content: Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis (RVVC) is a condition that affects up to 5% of women. Despite its prevalence, no comprehensive systematic review of treatments for RVVC has been published to date. The primary aim of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of both pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatments for RVVC. A secondary aim was to assess patient preferences regarding treatment options. To gather data, electronic searches were conducted in databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL, with the last search performed on October 6, 2021. Additionally, reference lists of identified trials were manually reviewed, and authors of trials, RVVC experts, and manufacturers of related products were contacted for further information. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated treatments for RVVC over a minimum duration of six months. Eligible participants were women who had experienced four or more symptomatic episodes of vulvovaginal candidiasis in the past year. Women with immunosuppressive disorders or those taking immunosuppressant medications were excluded, but women with diabetes mellitus and pregnant women were included. Diagnosis of RVVC was confirmed through the presence of symptoms and a positive culture and/or microscopy. Both drug-based and non-drug therapies, as well as partner treatments, were considered. The primary outcomes assessed were: (1) the number of clinical recurrences per participant per year, (2) the proportion of participants with at least one clinical recurrence during the treatment and follow-up period, and (3) adverse events. Two authors independently reviewed the titles and abstracts of studies to identify eligible trials. Data extraction was performed independently by two authors, and the risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. A fixed-effects model was used for data pooling, with results expressed as risk ratios (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). In cases of significant statistical heterogeneity (I² > 70%), data were not pooled, or a random-effects model was used (I² = 40-70%). The GRADE tool was employed to evaluate the overall certainty of evidence for the primary outcomes. A total of 23 studies involving 2,212 women aged 17 to 67 years met the inclusion criteria. Most studies excluded pregnant women and those with diabetes or immunosuppression. The predominant fungal species identified was Candida albicans. The included studies were generally small, with fewer than 100 participants each. Six studies compared antifungal treatments with placebo (607 participants), four studies compared oral antifungals with topical antifungals (543 participants), and one study compared different oral antifungal agents (45 participants). Other studies examined various dosing regimens, treatment durations, partner treatments, complementary therapies (e.g., Lactobacillus vaginal tablets, probiotics), and alternative interventions (e.g., Dermasilk briefs versus cotton briefs, Lactobacillus vaccination versus heliotherapy versus ciclopiroxolamine). No studies directly compared different topical antifungal agents. Nine studies reported industry funding, three were funded independently, and eleven did not disclose their funding sources. The overall risk of bias in the studies was high or unclear, primarily due to inadequate blinding of allocation and participants, as well as poor reporting practices. Meta-analyses of drug treatments (oral and topical) compared to placebo or no treatment suggested a potential reduction in clinical recurrences at six months (RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.63; number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome [NNTB] = 2; 607 participants; six studies; I² = 82%; low-certainty evidence) and at 12 months (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.89; NNTB = 6; 585 participants; six studies; I² = 21%; low-certainty evidence). However, no studies reported the number of clinical recurrences per participant per year. The evidence regarding whether oral antifungal treatments compared to topical treatments increase or decrease the risk of clinical recurrence at six months (RR 1.66, 95% CI 0.83 to 3.31; 206 participants; three studies; I² = 0%; very low-certainty evidence) or at 12 months (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.27; 206 participants; three studies; I² = 10%; very low-certainty evidence) was very uncertain. Adverse events were infrequent across both treatment and control groups, but the reporting of adverse events was inconsistent, of very low quality, and could not be pooled. Overall, the rate of adverse events was low, ranging from less than 5% to no reported side effects or complications. In conclusion, oral or topical antifungal treatments may reduce symptomatic clinical recurrences in women with RVVC when compared to placebo or no treatment. However, no clear differences were identified between various treatment options, such as oral versus topical treatments or different doses and durations. These findings are not applicable to pregnant women, immunocompromised women, or women with diabetes, as these populations were not adequately represented in the studies. Further research is needed to determine the optimal medication, dose, and frequency for treating RVVC.
